name: Manuel Santana
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1961 French Championships (Grand Slam singles title) at age 23, becoming the first Spaniard to win a major.
early_history_summary: Santana grew up in Madrid as the son of a tennis club groundskeeper and began his career as a ball boy at the Madrid Country Club at age 10, developing remarkable hand-eye coordination. He won the Spanish junior championships in 1955 and 1956, made his Davis Cup debut at 19, and within two years claimed his first Grand Slam title at Roland Garros in 1961.
family_context_summary: Son of a groundskeeper at a tennis club in Madrid; grew up in a working-class family during the Franco era, where tennis was considered an elite sport.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father worked at a tennis club, providing incidental proximity to the sport, though not as a player or coach.
primary_early_advantage_tags: ball-boy immersion, club access, early specialization, working-class outsider
evidence_summary: Santana's father was a groundskeeper at the Madrid Country Club, giving the young Santana access to tennis as a ball boy from age 10. He developed exceptional hand-eye coordination and tactical skills through daily immersion at the club, winning junior championships by his late teens. His working-class background in Franco-era Spain made his entry into an elite sport unusual, but the club environment provided both facilities and competitive exposure that catalyzed his rapid rise to a Grand Slam title by age 23.
starting_point: Born to a working-class family in Madrid; father was a groundskeeper at a tennis club, and Santana began as a ball boy to earn extra money.
current_position: Died in December 2021 at age 83 in Marbella, Spain; final role was tennis tournament director and legend of Spanish tennis.

trajectory.event: Won the Spanish junior tennis championships, establishing himself as a promising young player.
Made Davis Cup debut for Spain, beginning a record-setting national team career.
Won the French Championships, becoming the first Spaniard to win a Grand Slam singles title.
Won his second French Championships title, defeating Nicola Pietrangeli in the final.
Won the US Championships and achieved the world No. 1 ranking.
Won Wimbledon, the first Spaniard to do so, becoming a national hero.
Inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame.
Died on December 11, 2021, in Marbella, Spain.

name: Nikocado Avocado
milestone_by_age_26: Fame arrived after age 26; his first mukbang video in September 2016 (age 24) reached only ~50,000 views, and his breakout to millions of subscribers occurred in 2019-2020 (ages 27-28). No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born in Ukraine and adopted by an American family, Perry grew up in Pennsylvania and pursued violin performance at the Catholic University of America. He worked as a freelance violinist and Home Depot worker before starting a YouTube channel in 2014 focused on vegan lifestyle content, which gained little traction.
family_context_summary: Adopted in infancy from Ukraine by an American family in Pennsylvania; struggled with mental health issues from a young age.
evidence_summary: Perry was adopted from Ukraine and raised in Pennsylvania, studying violin performance in college before pivoting to YouTube. His channel started in 2014 with vegan content but gained minimal traction until his September 2016 video about leaving veganism, which reached ~50,000 views. His explosive growth to millions of subscribers occurred in 2019-2020, well after age 26.

name: Rickson Gracie
milestone_by_age_26: Defeated the 230-pound feared vale tudo fighter Rei Zulu in a high-profile match in Brasilia in 1980 at age 20, gaining immediate national recognition in Brazil as the Gracie family's top fighter.
early_history_summary: Born into the Gracie jiu-jitsu dynasty as the son of co-founder Hélio Gracie, Rickson began training at age 6 and was teaching by 15. He received his black belt at 18 and by 20 was the family's designated champion, defeating the much larger Rei Zulu in a nationally publicized vale tudo match.
family_context_summary: Son of Hélio Gracie, co-founder of Brazilian jiu-jitsu; born into the preeminent martial arts family in Brazil, with training beginning in infancy.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Hélio Gracie was the co-founder of BJJ and personally trained Rickson from childhood; the entire Gracie family was immersed in martial arts.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Gracie dynasty, father-mentor, early black belt, family fighting legacy, sibling training partners
evidence_summary: Rickson Gracie was born into the founding family of Brazilian jiu-jitsu, with his father Hélio Gracie personally training him from age 6. He received his black belt at 18 and was teaching by 15, accumulating thousands of hours of mat time before his breakthrough fight at 20. The Gracie family ecosystem provided elite training partners (brothers Rorion, Relson, Royce), a established martial arts academy, and the family's reputation as fighters, making Rickson the designated champion of the clan by his late teens.
starting_point: Born in Rio de Janeiro as the son of Hélio Gracie, co-founder of Brazilian jiu-jitsu, into the preeminent martial arts family in Brazil.
current_position: Retired mixed martial artist and 9th-degree red belt in BJJ; runs the Rickson Gracie Jiu-Jitsu Association; estimated net worth not publicly documented; resides in the United States.

trajectory.event: Received black belt in Brazilian jiu-jitsu from his father Hélio Gracie.
Defeated 230-pound vale tudo fighter Rei Zulu in Brasilia, gaining national recognition in Brazil.
Defeated Rei Zulu again in a rematch at Maracanazinho Stadium before 20,000 spectators.
Moved to the United States to help establish the first Gracie Jiu-Jitsu Academy in Torrance, California.
Won Vale Tudo Japan 1994, defeating three opponents by submission in a single night.
Headlined Pride 1, defeating Nobuhiko Takada by submission in the first round.
Promoted to ninth-degree red belt, the second-highest ranking in Brazilian jiu-jitsu.

name: Alain Aspect
milestone_by_age_26: Fame arrived with his Bell test experiments in 1980-1982 (age 33-35) and the 2022 Nobel Prize; by age 26 he had only completed standard academic qualifications (agrégation 1969, master's thesis 1971) with no material independently verifiable career milestone.
early_history_summary: Aspect studied at the École Normale Supérieure de Cachan and Université d'Orsay, passing the agrégation in physics in 1969 and completing a master's thesis in 1971. He then taught in Cameroon for three years before beginning his doctoral work on Bell's inequality experiments in 1974.
evidence_summary: Aspect passed the agrégation in physics in 1969 and completed a master's thesis in 1971, both standard academic qualifications. His groundbreaking Bell test experiments, which would earn him the Nobel Prize, were conducted in the early 1980s when he was in his mid-30s. No material career milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Krzysztof Komeda
milestone_by_age_26: Achieved breakthrough success at the I Sopot Jazz Festival in August 1956 at age 25, establishing himself as a leading figure in Polish jazz.
early_history_summary: Komeda took piano lessons from early childhood and attended the Poznań conservatory before World War II disrupted his training. He studied medicine at the Medical Academy in Poznań, obtaining his MD in 1956, while simultaneously playing jazz in the underground 'catacomb period' of Polish jazz, culminating in his breakthrough at the 1956 Sopot Jazz Festival.
family_context_summary: Born in Poznań to parents Mieczysław and Zenobia; took music lessons from early childhood and attended the Poznań conservatory before the war disrupted his education.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond early music lessons; family supported early conservatory training.
primary_early_advantage_tags: early conservatory training, catacomb jazz scene, peer network, dual medicine-music path
evidence_summary: Komeda began piano lessons in early childhood and attended the Poznań conservatory, though World War II interrupted his formal training for six years. He pursued medicine while simultaneously immersing himself in Poland's underground jazz scene, jamming with key musicians like Witold Kujawski and Andrzej Trzaskowski in Cracow. His breakthrough at the 1956 Sopot Jazz Festival at age 25 established him as a pioneer of modern Polish jazz, leading to film scoring work with Roman Polanski starting in 1957.
starting_point: Born in Poznań, Poland to parents Mieczysław and Zenobia; took piano lessons from early childhood and attended the Poznań conservatory before WWII disrupted his education.
current_position: Died in April 1969 at age 37 in Warsaw; final work was the score for Roman Polanski's Rosemary's Baby (1968).

trajectory.event: Breakthrough performance at the I Sopot Jazz Festival, establishing himself as a leading figure in Polish jazz.
Composed his first film score for Roman Polanski's short film Two Men and a Wardrobe.
Scored Polanski's feature debut Knife in the Water, which received an Academy Award nomination.
Released Astigmatic, widely considered one of the most important European jazz albums.
Composed the score for Polanski's Rosemary's Baby in Hollywood.
Died on April 23, 1969, in Warsaw from injuries sustained in a tragic accident in Los Angeles.

name: Franca Viola
milestone_by_age_26: Became the first Italian woman to publicly refuse a reparatory marriage to her rapist, resulting in a high-profile trial in December 1966 at age 18 that made her a national symbol of women's emancipation.
early_history_summary: Born to a farming family in Alcamo, Sicily, Viola was abducted and raped by her former fiancé Filippo Melodia in December 1965 at age 17. Supported by her father Bernardo, she refused the traditional 'matrimonio riparatore' that would have absolved her rapist, leading to a nationally publicized trial in December 1966.
family_context_summary: Daughter of Bernardo and Vita Viola, farmers (coltivatori diretti) in Alcamo, Sicily; the family was of modest means with some vineyard land. Her father's steadfast support was critical to her decision to refuse the reparatory marriage.
parent_family_domain_summary: Farming family with no particular domain expertise relevant to activism; father Bernardo's courage in supporting Franca against mafia-linked intimidation was pivotal.
primary_early_advantage_tags: paternal support, adversity catalyst, cultural defiance, Sicilian gender norms
evidence_summary: Viola was born to a modest farming family in Alcamo, Sicily. Her abduction and rape at 17 by a mafia-linked former fiancé, and her subsequent refusal to marry him, defied deep-seated Southern Italian conventions. Her father Bernardo's unwavering support enabled her to press charges, resulting in a landmark 1966 trial that made her a symbol of women's emancipation in post-war Italy. The adversity she faced was the direct catalyst for her national prominence.
starting_point: Born to a modest farming family (coltivatori diretti) in Alcamo, Sicily; father Bernardo was a farmer with some vineyard land.
current_position: Living privately in Alcamo, Sicily; married Giuseppe Ruisi and became a symbol of women's emancipation in Italy; honored by Italian President Sergio Mattarella.

trajectory.event: Abducted and raped by former fiancé Filippo Melodia on December 26, 1965, in Alcamo, Sicily.
Became the first Italian woman to publicly refuse a reparatory marriage, resulting in a high-profile trial in December 1966.
Melodia was convicted and sentenced to 11 years in prison; Viola's defiance became a national symbol.
Article 544 of the Italian criminal code, which allowed reparatory marriage, was finally repealed, partly attributed to Viola's case.
Honored as a Grand Officer of the Order of Merit of the Italian Republic by President Giorgio Napolitano.

name: Jan Raas
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Dutch National Road Race Championship in 1976 at age 23 and the Milan-San Remo Monument in 1977 at age 24, establishing himself as an elite classics specialist.
early_history_summary: Raas turned professional in 1975 with TI-Raleigh and quickly established himself as a gifted sprinter and classics specialist. He won the Dutch National Road Race Championship in 1976, then claimed his first Monument at Milan-San Remo in 1977, followed by the first of his five Amstel Gold Race victories the same year.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond being born in Heinkenszand, Netherlands.
primary_early_advantage_tags: TI-Raleigh team, Peter Post mentorship, Dutch cycling ecosystem, sprinter talent
evidence_summary: Raas turned professional in 1975 with TI-Raleigh, a top Dutch cycling team, under the mentorship of director Peter Post. His natural sprinting ability and tactical sense led to rapid success: the Dutch National Championship in 1976 and his first Monument at Milan-San Remo in 1977, both before age 25. The Dutch cycling ecosystem and the strong TI-Raleigh team structure provided the competitive environment for his early breakthrough.
starting_point: Born in Heinkenszand, Netherlands; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Retired former professional cyclist and team manager; guided teams including Buckler and Rabobank; served as Netherlands national cycling coach.

trajectory.event: Turned professional with TI-Raleigh, beginning his elite cycling career.
Won the Dutch National Road Race Championship, the first of three national titles.
Won Milan-San Remo, his first Monument, and the first of five Amstel Gold Race victories.
Won the World Road Race Championship in Valkenburg and the Tour of Flanders.
Won Paris-Roubaix, cementing his status as one of the great classics riders.
Retired from professional cycling and transitioned to team management.

name: Brice Oligui Nguema
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; he trained at Meknes Royal Military Academy in 1997 (age 22) and served in early military roles, but his significant appointments (aide-de-camp to President Omar Bongo, head of Republican Guard) came after age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in Haut-Ogooué Province, Gabon, to a military officer father and Teke mother, Oligui studied at Omar Bongo University before training at the Meknes Royal Military Academy in Morocco in 1997. He served in early military roles in Gabon's Republican Guard but did not achieve a material career milestone by age 26.
family_context_summary: Son of a Fang military officer and Teke mother; member of the extended Bongo family; raised primarily by his mother in Haut-Ogooué Province, a Bongo family stronghold.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a military officer, providing a career model; maternal connection to the Bongo political dynasty offered proximity to power.
evidence_summary: Oligui was born into a family with military and political connections in Gabon, being a maternal cousin of Ali Bongo. He trained at the Meknes Royal Military Academy in Morocco in 1997 and served in the Republican Guard, but his significant appointments — aide-de-camp to President Omar Bongo and later head of the Republican Guard — came after age 26. No material career milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Nikola Pilić
milestone_by_age_26: Reached the Wimbledon doubles final in 1962 at age 22, unseeded, defeating the reigning champions and top seeds Roy Emerson and Neale Fraser in the semifinals.
early_history_summary: Pilić took up tennis at age 13 in 1952 at the Firule tennis club in Split, training on clay courts while studying shipbuilding. Within four years he was representing Yugoslavia's junior team, and by 1962 he reached the Wimbledon doubles final unseeded with compatriot Boro Jovanović, sensationally defeating the top seeds.
family_context_summary: Born in Split, Yugoslavia (now Croatia) to Krsto Pilić and Danica Tomić-Ferić; family described as close-knit and outdoorsy but not affluent.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no evidence of family tennis background.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Firule club access, Yugoslav junior team, doubles partnership, late start rapid rise
evidence_summary: Pilić started tennis relatively late at age 13 but trained obsessively at the Firule tennis club in Split, quickly rising to represent Yugoslavia's junior team within four years. His partnership with Boro Jovanović in doubles proved potent, leading to a stunning Wimbledon doubles final in 1962 where they defeated the top seeds. The Yugoslav tennis association covered his travel expenses, and the Firule club provided the clay courts and competitive environment for his development.
starting_point: Born in Split, Yugoslavia (now Croatia) to Krsto Pilić and Danica Tomić-Ferić; a close-knit, outdoorsy family of modest means.
current_position: Died in September 2025 at age 86; final role was legendary tennis coach who led three countries to Davis Cup titles and trained Novak Djokovic.

trajectory.event: Began playing tennis at the Firule tennis club in Split, Yugoslavia.
Represented Yugoslavia's junior tennis team, showing rapid improvement.
Reached the Wimbledon doubles final unseeded with Boro Jovanović, defeating top seeds Emerson and Fraser.
Won the Moscow International Championships in singles.
Reached Wimbledon singles semifinals, beating second seed Roy Emerson.
Signed with Lamar Hunt's World Championship Tennis as one of the 'Handsome Eight' professional players.
Won the US Open men's doubles title with Pierre Barthes, defeating Newcombe and Laver.
Reached the French Open singles final; his suspension sparked the Wimbledon players' boycott.

name: Piet Keizer
milestone_by_age_26: Made his Ajax first-team debut on February 5, 1961 at age 17 and became a regular starter, establishing himself as a key player for one of Europe's most important clubs by his late teens.
early_history_summary: Keizer joined Ajax's youth academy in 1955 at age 12 after playing for amateur club Amstel. He made his first-team debut at 17 in February 1961 against Feyenoord and quickly became known for his devastating wing play and crosses, forming a lethal partnership with Johan Cruyff in the mid-1960s.
family_context_summary: Born and raised in Amsterdam; joined Ajax youth academy at age 12. Family background beyond this is not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Ajax youth academy, early debut, Amsterdam football ecosystem, Cruyff partnership
evidence_summary: Keizer joined Ajax's youth academy at age 12 in 1955, receiving structured training in one of Europe's most important football clubs. He made his first-team debut at 17 under coach Vic Buckingham and quickly became a regular, known for his dribbling and crossing ability. The Ajax ecosystem in Amsterdam provided elite-level training, competitive matches, and eventually the partnership with Johan Cruyff that defined the Total Football era. By age 26, he had already been a first-team regular for nearly a decade and reached the European Cup final in 1969.
starting_point: Born and raised in Amsterdam; joined the Ajax youth academy at age 12 in 1955 after playing for amateur club Amstel.
current_position: Died on February 10, 2017 at age 73 in Amsterdam; final role was scout and technical adviser to Ajax after retiring from playing in 1974.

trajectory.event: Joined the Ajax youth academy, beginning his lifelong association with the club.
Made his Ajax first-team debut on February 5 against Feyenoord, beginning a 14-year senior career.
Made his debut for the Netherlands national team.
Became a key player under new manager Rinus Michels as Ajax began its rise to European dominance.
Reached the European Cup final with Ajax, losing 4-1 to AC Milan.
Won the first of three consecutive European Cups with Ajax, providing a key assist in the final.
Retired from professional football after 489 official matches for Ajax.

name: Jannis Kounellis
milestone_by_age_26: Had his first solo exhibition at Galleria La Tartaruga in Rome in 1960 at age 24, presenting his seminal Alfabeto works that launched his career as a pioneering contemporary artist.
early_history_summary: Born in Piraeus, Greece, Kounellis moved to Rome in 1956 at age 20 to study at the Accademia di Belle Arti. While still a student, he had his first solo show at Galleria La Tartaruga in 1960, presenting black-and-white canvases stenciled with letters and numbers, marking the beginning of his radical departure from traditional painting.
family_context_summary: Born in Piraeus, Greece, to a family of seafarers; grew up during World War II and the Greek Civil War before relocating to Rome at age 20.
parent_family_domain_summary: Family of seafarers in the port city of Piraeus; no direct art world connection, but the industrial port environment later influenced his use of raw materials.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Rome art scene, Accademia di Belle Arti, Galleria La Tartaruga, postwar displacement
evidence_summary: Kounellis was born into a seafaring family in Piraeus, Greece, and experienced World War II and the Greek Civil War before moving to Rome at 20 to study art. His enrollment at the Accademia di Belle Arti placed him in the heart of Rome's contemporary art scene, where he was influenced by Lucio Fontana and Alberto Burri. His first solo show at Galleria La Tartaruga in 1960 at age 24 launched his career, leading to his association with the Arte Povera movement by 1967.
starting_point: Born in Piraeus, Greece, to a family of seafarers; experienced WWII and the Greek Civil War before relocating to Rome in 1956 to study art.
current_position: Died on February 16, 2017 at age 80 in Rome; final status was one of the most influential figures of the Arte Povera movement with works in major international museum collections.

trajectory.event: Moved from Greece to Rome and enrolled at the Accademia di Belle Arti.
Had his first solo exhibition at Galleria La Tartaruga in Rome, presenting the Alfabeto works.
Began introducing found objects into his artworks, expanding beyond traditional painting.
Participated in the landmark Arte Povera exhibition in Genoa curated by Germano Celant.
Installed twelve live horses in a gallery, his most famous work, bringing international recognition.
Had his first solo show in New York at the Sonnabend Gallery.
Died on February 16, 2017, in Rome, Italy.

name: Leonardo DiCaprio
milestone_by_age_26: Received an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor for What's Eating Gilbert Grape at age 19 in 1994, making him the seventh-youngest nominee in that category.
early_history_summary: DiCaprio began acting in television commercials and series as a teenager in Los Angeles, landing roles in Growing Pains and Parenthood. His film breakthrough came with This Boy's Life (1993) opposite Robert De Niro, followed by his acclaimed performance in What's Eating Gilbert Grape (1993), which earned him an Oscar nomination at 19.
family_context_summary: Son of George DiCaprio, an underground comix writer/editor and distributor, and Irmelin Indenbirken, a German-born legal secretary; parents divorced when he was a toddler but both remained involved in his upbringing and career.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father George was deeply embedded in the underground arts/comix scene of 1970s-80s Los Angeles, providing creative guidance and script screening for Leonardo's early career.
primary_early_advantage_tags: LA film ecosystem, father's arts network, early TV reps, audition culture, De Niro mentorship
evidence_summary: DiCaprio grew up in Los Angeles with a father active in the underground comix scene and a mother who supported his acting ambitions from a young age. His father screened scripts and guided his early role choices, while the Los Angeles entertainment ecosystem provided access to auditions and TV roles from his early teens. By 19, he had landed a breakthrough role opposite Robert De Niro in This Boy's Life and earned an Oscar nomination for What's Eating Gilbert Grape, establishing him as one of the most promising young actors of his generation.
starting_point: Born in Los Angeles to George DiCaprio, an underground comix writer/editor, and Irmelin Indenbirken, a German-born legal secretary; parents divorced when he was a toddler but co-parented his early career.
current_position: Academy Award-winning actor and producer; founder of Appian Way Productions and the Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation; estimated net worth ~$300M; resides in Los Angeles.

trajectory.event: Landed recurring TV roles in Growing Pains and Parenthood, building early acting experience.
Starred in This Boy's Life opposite Robert De Niro and What's Eating Gilbert Grape, earning an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor.
Starred in Titanic, which became the highest-grossing film at the time, achieving worldwide fame.
Starred in Gangs of New York, beginning his long collaboration with director Martin Scorsese.
Nominated for Best Actor Oscar for The Aviator, solidifying his status as a leading man.
Won the Academy Award for Best Actor for The Revenant after multiple nominations.
Continues as one of Hollywood's most bankable stars and a prominent environmental activist.
